title: A Clock for the Letter
premise: In 1848, in a river town on the edge of uprising, August Hartwell works the type cases of her father's print shop, convinced that history is something printed about other people. When a wounded stranger arrives bearing letters written in the unmistakable hand of her brother Tomas — executed by the government two years ago — she discovers he lives, hiding among conspirators who forged his death to protect him. As the revolution ignites and the authorities close in, August must smuggle evidence of a magistrate's massacre to sympathetic printers abroad, but there is only one berth on the last boat out: her father, whose failing memory makes him useless to the cause but precious to her heart, or Tomas, whose testimony could convict the magistrate and free the town. She chooses her father, forging Tomas's handwriting one last time to send him into exile believing it was his own idea; Tomas stays, testifies, and dies at dawn as the revolution briefly triumphs. Years later, August cuts a new typeface in his name and prints the truth that outlived them all.
about_author: Rafael Delacroix is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century print shops across Eastern Europe before turning to fiction. Their novels examine how ordinary craftspeople become accidental witnesses to history.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: August Hartwell sorts type in her father Elias's print shop, cataloguing his growing forgetfulness while the town murmurs of unrest. Her POV establishes her belief that revolutions are ink for other papers. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Loading Door
chapters.summary: A feverish man named Corvin collapses at the shop's back door clutching satchels of contraband pamphlets. August hides him from a patrol. His POV reveals he carries letters signed by Tomas Hartwell — a man officially dead two years. Beat: shock cracking open a sealed grief.

chapters.title: Handwriting of the Dead
chapters.summary: August confronts Corvin with the letters; the looping g's and crossed t's are undeniably Tomas's. He explains the conspiracy faked the execution to protect witnesses to Magistrate Voss's massacre. August's POV, torn between hope and fury at being deceived. Beat: vertigo of impossible proof.

chapters.title: What Father Remembers
chapters.summary: Elias, lucid for an hour, recalls printing the original death notice and suspects it was coerced. August realizes her father may have unknowingly abetted the cover-up. Elias's POV, memory flickering like bad type. Beat: guilt inherited without consent.

chapters.title: The Committee of the Undersigned
chapters.summary: Corvin brings August to the conspirators' cellar press, where she sees Tomas's name on their roster but not the man himself. Their leader, Ilsa, tests her loyalty with a dangerous errand. August's POV. Beat: seduction of belonging to something larger.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Fingernails
chapters.summary: August runs the errand — smuggling a plate inside a coffin shipment — and glimpses a hooded figure she believes is Tomas, who flees rather than face her. Her POV, anger sharpening. Beat: rejection that wounds deeper than the lie.

chapters.title: Voss Summons the Printers
chapters.summary: Magistrate Voss orders all presses registered and inspected; Elias's shop is first on the list. August hides the conspiracy's plates in the type cases' false bottoms. Alternating POVs of August and a nervous inspector, Brandt, who suspects more than he reports. Beat: the law becomes a predator.

chapters.title: A Brother Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Tomas finally appears, begging August to stop asking questions; his survival depends on Voss believing him dead. August demands the truth about the massacre he witnessed. Tomas's POV, shame and self-preservation at war. Beat: love curdling into accusation.

chapters.title: The Massacre at Millbridge Ford
chapters.summary: Tomas recounts what he saw: fourteen strikers drowned on Voss's order, himself the only witness who escaped. August understands why his testimony is worth more than his life. Shared flashback chapter, Tomas narrating. Beat: horror given a human face.

chapters.title: Barricades in the Rain
chapters.summary: Revolution erupts; students and printers raise barricades. The cellar press prints declarations through the night, August setting type beside Ilsa. August's POV. Beat: history no longer happening elsewhere — it is under her fingers.

chapters.title: Brandt's Choice
chapters.summary: Inspector Brandt, ordered to raid the cellar, instead burns his own report and warns them, then deserts. His POV, a minor man choosing conscience over career. Beat: justice begins as small disobedience.

chapters.title: The List of Fourteen
chapters.summary: Ilsa reveals the plan: get Tomas's sworn testimony plus the victims' names to printers abroad before Voss retakes the town. One berth remains on the last boat. August's POV, the choice taking shape. Beat: hope with a price tag.

chapters.title: Elias Wanders
chapters.summary: Elias disappears during the chaos; August finds him at the riverbank trying to deliver a newspaper to Tomas 'before the boy misses supper,' his mind years behind. August's POV. Beat: tenderness that makes the coming choice unbearable.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Berth
chapters.summary: August argues with herself in a sleepless night: Tomas's testimony could convict Voss but will kill him; Elias can be saved but remembers nothing worth saving. Ilsa pressures her to choose Tomas. August's POV. Beat: the novel's moral fulcrum.

chapters.title: Voss Retakes the Town
chapters.summary: Government troops crush the uprising; the cellar press is smashed, Ilsa captured, Corvin killed covering the retreat. August escapes with the testimony plates. Multiple POVs in rapid succession. Beat: triumph inverted into catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Forgery
chapters.summary: August forges a letter in Tomas's hand ordering himself to stay and fight, while telling Elias the boat is for him alone — letting each believe the decision was made above her. August's POV, hands steady, heart not. Beat: loyalty and truth fused into a single act of deception.

chapters.title: Last Boat at Dawn
chapters.summary: At the dock, Elias boards; Tomas arrives too late, reads the forged letter, and understands — meeting August's eyes across the water without a word. August's POV. Beat: devastating mutual recognition, forgiveness unspoken.

chapters.title: The Trial of Ilsa Reiner
chapters.summary: Tomas surrenders to testify at Ilsa's trial, naming Voss before the tribunal. Voss is convicted as the town falls back into uneasy order. Tomas's POV, calm acceptance. Beat: justice achieved at the cost the reader always feared.

chapters.title: Fourteen Bells
chapters.summary: Tomas is executed at dawn; the town rings bells fourteen times, once per victim. August, returned, stands in the crowd holding his last real letter. August's POV. Beat: grief transfigured into public memory.

chapters.title: Cutting a New Face
chapters.summary: August designs a typeface in Tomas's honor, carving punches through the winter while Elias declines gently, sometimes calling her by her brother's name. August's POV. Beat: mourning made into craft.

chapters.title: The Edition That Outlived Them
chapters.summary: August prints the full account of Millbridge Ford in the new face, distributing copies beyond Voss's successors' reach. Brandt returns to help set the final pages. August's POV. Beat: truth as inheritance.

chapters.title: A Clock for the Letter
chapters.summary: Years later, aged August teaches apprentices, including a girl who asks why the typeface is named for a dead man. August answers with the story — and winds the shop clock Tomas once repaired, which still keeps perfect time. August's POV closing frame. Beat: memory kept wound, ticking past all the deaths.
